auxiliary_material: The authors cite preclinical mechanisms where inosine enhances tumor cell immunogenicity via UBA6 inhibition and promotes T-cell activation through the adenosine 2A receptor. Safety data showed Grade 3-4 adverse reactions were slightly lower in the inosine group (29% vs 36%). The study design was a single-center, prospective, randomized, open-label Phase 2 trial (NCT05809336). The discussion notes that inosine is a known gut microbiota metabolite and a safe, low-cost adjuvant previously used for hepatitis.
outline_action: Search for pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) substudies or biomarker reports associated with this trial registration (NCT05809336) that may contain serum or tissue metabolite measurements. Broaden the search to observational cohort studies profiling baseline metabolomics in ICI-treated patients to find endogenous concentration ranges. Investigate whether other clinical trials of microbiome modulators (e.g., fecal transplant, specific probiotics) include metabolite concentration data correlated with response.
remaining_gap: The success criteria require absolute physiological concentrations (μM/ng/mL) of inosine or SCFAs in human tumor microenvironment or serum, which this study does not report. There is no measurement of baseline or on-treatment metabolite levels in patient samples, and thus no statistical correlation between endogenous metabolite concentrations and ORR/PFS is provided. Additionally, no data on short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is included. The current data links treatment assignment to outcome, not measured concentration to outcome.
useful_material: This study provides clinical evidence that oral inosine supplementation (0.2 g, three times/day) combined with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors significantly prolonged median progression-free survival (7.00 vs 4.40 months; HR 0.63, p = 0.011) compared to inhibitors alone in 172 patients with advanced solid tumors. Although the objective response rate (26.7% vs 15.1%) did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.061), the data establish a clinical association between exogenous inosine exposure and improved ICI outcomes (PFS). Subgroup analyses indicated stronger PFS benefits in lung cancer patients (HR 0.45) and those with specific inflammatory markers (e.g., LDH≥216, NLR<4), suggesting patient stratification factors relevant to metabolite efficacy.
